{{short description|Israeli historian of modern life sciences}}
'''Ute Deichmann''' ({{Langx|he|אוטה דייכמן}}) is an [[historian]] of modern life sciences.<ref name="Ben Gurion University of the Negev">{{cite web|title=Ute Deichmann|url=http://in.bgu.ac.il/en/loeb/Pages/uted.aspx|publisher=Ben Gurion University of the Negev|accessdate=16 April 2018}}</ref> She is adjunct full professor at [[Ben-Gurion University of the Negev]] in [[Israel]],<ref name="ResearchGate">{{cite web|title=Ute Deichmann|url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ute_Deichmann|accessdate=16 April 2018}}</ref> where she was the founding director of the Jacques Loeb Centre for the History and Philosophy of the Sciences in 2007 and continues to be the director.<ref name="LEO BAECK INSTITUTE LONDON">{{cite web|title=Research: Ute Deichmann|url=http://www.leobaeck.co.uk/invisible/research-ute-deichmann|publisher=LEO BAECK INSTITUTE LONDON|accessdate=16 April 2018}}</ref> She has also been an associate professor at the University of Cologne, Germany since 2011.

==Career==
Ute Deichmann received her Ph.D. in 1991 at the Department of [[Genetics]] of the [[University of Cologne]] with the thesis ''Biologists under Hitler: The Expulsion of Jewish Scientists and the Development of Biological Research in Germany''.<ref name="Biologists under Hitler">{{cite book|title=Biologists under Hitler|date=1996|publisher=Harvard University Press|location=Cambridge, MA|isbn=0-674-07404-1}}</ref> She received her habilitation in 2000 at the same university with a thesis on chemists and biochemists in the era of [[National Socialism]], published in 2001.<ref name="Flüchten, Mitmachen, Vergessen. Chemiker und Biochemiker im Nationalsozialismus">{{cite book|title=Flüchten, Mitmachen, Vergessen. Chemiker und Biochemiker im Nationalsozialismus|date=2001|publisher=Wiley-VCH, Weinheim|location=NY, NY}}</ref>  She later became head of a working group on the history of modern biology and chemistry in the same department at the University of Cologne.<ref name="PDF Working Group">{{cite web|last1=Deichmann|first1=Ute|title=Working group History and Philosophy of Modern Informational and Structural Biosciences|url=http://www.genetik.uni-koeln.de/groups/Deichmann/homepage-koeln-Dec04.2016.pdf|accessdate=15 May 2018}}</ref> From 2003 to 2007, she was a research professor at the Leo-Baeck-Institute in [[London]] where, together with Ulrich Charpa, she was the head of the project "Jews in German-Speaking Academia, 19th and 20th centuries".<ref name="Leo Baeck Institute London">{{cite web|title=Research: Ute Deichmann|url=http://www.leobaeck.co.uk/invisible/research-ute-deichmann|publisher=Leo Baeck Institute London|accessdate=15 May 2018}}</ref>  In 2007, Deichmann became founding director of the Jacques Loeb Centre for the History and Philosophy of the Life Sciences at [[Ben-Gurion University of the Negev]] in [[Beer Sheva]]. Since 2011, she has headed the center as an adjunct full professor.<ref name="Jacques Loeb Centre">{{cite web|title=Ute Deichmann|url=http://in.bgu.ac.il/en/loeb/Pages/uted.aspx|publisher=Jacques Loeb Centre|accessdate=15 May 2018}}</ref>

==Research==
Her research focuses on the history and philosophy of modern life sciences with an emphasis on:<ref name="Research Gate">{{cite web|title=Ute Deichmann|url=https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Ute_Deichmann|publisher=Research Gate|accessdate=15 May 2018}}</ref>  
*Tracing the origin of basic life sciences concepts such as biological specificity, hierarchy, genomic regulation, and epigenetics and how they have changed over time.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Deichmann|first1=Ute|title=Molecular" versus "Colloidal": Controversies in Biology and Biochemistry, 1900–1940|journal=Bulletin for the History of Chemistry |volume=32|date=2007|pages=105–118}}</ref>
*Philosophy and epistemology of research in the experimental life sciences from the 19th to the 21st century and the impact of scientific personalities. 
*Critically reviewing the methodology and philosophy behind scientific claims considered revolutionary by many scientists, but whose far-reaching implications were later rejected. Among them are biocolloidy in the early 20th century and extended epigenetics or the "epigenetics hype” in the 21st century.<ref name="Developmental Biology 416">{{cite journal|last1=Deichmann|first1=Ute|title=Epigenetics: The origin and evolution of a fashionable topic|journal=Developmental Biology |volume=416|date=2016|issue=1|pages=249–254|doi=10.1016/j.ydbio.2016.06.005|pmid=27291929|doi-access=free}}</ref>
   
From 1991-2003 she conducted major research on biology and chemistry in [[Nazi Germany]] and the forced emigration of Jewish scientists and developed a unique methodology for historical-political-scientific analysis.<ref name="Jacques Loeb Centre" />

==Awards==
She is the recipient of the Ladislaus Laszt Award of Ben-Gurion University (1995) for her book ''Biologists under Hitler'' and the recipient of the Gmelin Beilstein Medal of the Society of German Chemical Society (2005) for her book ''Flee, Collaborate, Forget''. In 2011, she was the recipient of the Outstanding Paper Award from the Division of the History of Chemistry of the [[American Chemical Society]] for her article “‘Molecular’ versus ‘Colloidal’: Controversies in Biology and Biochemistry, 1900-1940”.<ref name="Euro Jewish Studies">{{cite web|title=Deichmann, Professor Ute|url=https://www.eurojewishstudies.org/directory/scholar-display/?idscholar=631|publisher=Euro Jewish Studies|accessdate=16 April 2018}}</ref><ref name="The Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities">{{cite web|title=Guest lecture: Prof. Ute Deichmann on "The Beginnings of Israeli-German Collaboration in the Sciences; Motives, Scientific Benefits and Hidden Agendas"|url=https://www.academy.ac.il/Index/Entry.aspx?nodeId=936&entryId=20033|publisher=The Israel Academy of Sciences and Humanities|accessdate=16 April 2018}}</ref>

* 2010. ''Chemistry and Engineering Life around 1900 - Research and Reflections by Jacques Loeb''. Biological Theory 4(4): 323–332.

* 2007. ''“Molecular” versus “Colloidal”: Controversies in Biology and Biochemistry, 1900–1940''. Bulletin for the History of Chemistry 32: 105–118.
* 2004. ''Early Responses to Avery's et al.’s 1944 Paper on DNA as Hereditary Material''. Historical Studies in the Physical and Biological Sciences 34:2, 207–233.
